newsitem.title: MEXICO: RTRS-Olympics-Samaranch sparks confusion with Sydney remark.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Olympics-Samaranch sparks confusion with Sydney remark.

text.p: IOC president Joan Antonio Samaranch sparked a flurry of confusion on Saturday when he said he was "not impressed" with a presentation made by the 2000 Sydney Olympics organisers.

Asked by a reporter at this Mexican Caribbean resort, where the IOC is meeting for four days, whether he was impressed by the Sydney presentation, Samaranch replied: "Not impressed, but we were very pleased, things are going well."
He went on to praise the preparations for the Sydney Summer Games.
IOC officials hurried to correct any impression that Samaranch was being critical of the Sydney report, adducing linguistic nuance and press cluster tactics to explain his remark.
"He never meant to be not impressed," IOC director general Francois Carrard said. "We had an excellent report by the Sydney organising committee."

Describing Samaranch as having been "caught abruptly...by a storm of journalists", Carrard said that as a Spanish speaker for whom English is not a first language "for him the word 'impressed' is anything sensational."
The Spanish cognate word "impresionado" has a stronger meaning than in English and can be positive or negative. It does not carry the favourable implication of the English word.

In other remarks to reporters, Samaranch said the Sydney Games would be smaller than Atlanta after a cap of 10,200 athletes was agreed with the organisers. "In Sydney we will have 500 athletes less and two sports more," he said.
Samaranch said earlier this week that 10,700 athletes went to Atlanta, although not all of them competed. Taekwondo and the triathlon have been added to the Sydney sports programme.
Olympics Minister Michael Knight, who heads the Sydney organising committee, said that the IOC board "seemed very pleased with our progress".
He said a tender would be announced for construction of the Olympic village before Christmas and ground would be broken some time in the first half of next year.

Carrard said the IOC on Saturday had approved a proposal to introduce a new, simpler accreditation system for the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics, in the hope of avoiding delays for athletes, officials and media of the kind seen in Atlanta.
The proposal will merge the existing Olympic identification card and separate accreditation card into a single document which will be got to Olympic participants earlier.
"We want to accelerate, simplify and if possible reduce the cost," Carrard said. "It is less difficult to test a new system for the Winter Olympics rather than the Summer Games."

Carrard also said that marketing and licensing arrangements for the 2002 Salt Lake City Winter Games were close to completion. IOC officials had been concerned at delays in formalising the agreements.
